en.content:
Hong Kong’s latest survey finding—that only 23% of residents want to have children—lands as a blunt reflection of a society that is, understandably, weighed down by cost pressures. If most respondents point to economic burden as the biggest obstacle, the message is not simply about personal preference. It is about the cumulative impact of housing affordability, day-to-day living costs, and uncertainty about career prospects—factors that can reshape family planning decisions even among those who still value parenthood. In that sense, the figure is less a cultural indictment than a diagnosis of structural constraints.

At the same time, it is worth looking beyond the headline number. A desire to have children is not only a matter of income, but also of time, housing stability, childcare availability, and the perceived feasibility of balancing work with family life. When these supports are perceived as insufficient, people may delay, reduce, or give up plans altogether—especially in an urban environment where households often face intense financial trade-offs. The question, therefore, is not merely how to encourage “more births,” but how to make family life practically sustainable for ordinary residents.

Policy debates should also be careful not to treat demographic challenges as a one-off public relations exercise. Long-term solutions typically require a coherent package: affordable and accessible childcare; employment arrangements that reduce the career penalty of having children; targeted assistance for young families; and housing policies that improve stability rather than merely compress short-term costs. These are areas where incremental improvement can matter greatly to household decisions—because what residents need most is predictability, not just one-time subsidies.

Finally, there is an important social dimension: demographic decline can affect not only the future workforce and fiscal outlook, but also community vitality and intergenerational solidarity. Addressing the low intention to have children should therefore be framed as a quality-of-life agenda—strengthening the conditions for raising children with dignity and security—rather than as a narrow numbers game. With that balanced approach, Hong Kong can respond to the challenge with realism, empathy, and effectiveness, in line with the wider goal of building a stable, resilient society.

zh.content:
香港呢代人對「要唔要生小朋友」嘅答案愈來愈清晰：調查話只有約23%港人有呢個意願，而主要阻力竟係經濟壓力。數字背後其實唔止係個人選擇，更反映一個結構性困局——樓價、租金、教育成本同養育支出長期偏高，令「建立家庭」變咗一種高門檻嘅奢侈品；同時，工作保障與向上流動感不足，又令未來更難估算。當社會講到人口政策，只討論口號或短期津貼，往往都同真正嘅壓力源頭擦唔到邊。

不過，我哋亦要理解：要人口回升唔係單靠逼人「要生」，而係要令願意生嘅家庭覺得可負擔、可預期、有人支援。經濟焦慮之所以持續，關鍵唔單在於一時嘅物價，而在於長期資源分配——例如托兒與學前支援不足、私營服務收費缺乏制衡、以及公共房屋供應與家庭需要之間嘅落差。若政府只以「鼓勵」取代「重整」，只會令調查結果由「想唔想生」變成「點樣先有能力生」。

因此更關鍵嘅，是要以政策設計回應「成本—時間—風險」三件事。成本方面，需要把育兒相關支出（托兒、醫療、教育銜接）逐步變得更可預測、更透明，並且避免只惠及少部分階層；時間方面，要讓照顧責任唔會被迫轉嫁到女性單一身上，透過更實際嘅彈性工作、育嬰安排同社區支援縮短家庭面對壓力嘅時間；風險方面，亦要用制度去降低失業或工時波動對養育計劃嘅打擊，例如更穩定嘅保障與可承受嘅再培訓支援。

話雖如此，人口議題終究要同社會精神狀態一齊睇。當年輕人覺得「努力都未必改善」，就算有家庭價值觀，亦會選擇暫停或放棄生育。今次調查其實係一面鏡：唔係話港人冷漠，而係話環境唔夠讓人安心。若要扭轉趨勢，政府就要承認問題存在於結構，而唔係把責任歸咎個人選擇；同時，社會亦應討論如何令「可養育」成為一種普遍能力，而唔係少數人先享有嘅回報。
